chapter_theme: The close of the Vimalaiyar ilampakam: the merchant Sagaradattan tells Civakan that a prophecy made at his daughter's birth, that her husband would make the unsold cargo sell, is fulfilled, gives him Vimalai, and the chapter follows their union through one night to the dawn when Civakan, promising a quick return, leaves her in tears.

cast.role: the hero, son of Saccandan and Vijayai, here married to Vimalai; called மைந்தன், காளை, வேலினான் in these verses
the merchant, Vimalai's father, named in 1973; called நாய்கன் here
Sagaradattan's daughter by Kamalai, whom Civakan marries
the women of Vimalai's house who play the dawn music

1974.reading: The merchant greets Civakan as Fortune itself come to his house, tells the warrior of the spear that this place is his, and the youth goes up into the red-gold house with the man who is to be his father-in-law.
1974.nuance: The narrator already calls the merchant மாமன் (line 4, as divided இல் மாமனொடு) before any word of marriage is spoken: the match is settled in the telling before it is offered.
1974.event: Sagaradattan welcomes Civakan as Fortune come in person and takes him up into his golden house.

1975.reading: The merchant asks Civakan to listen a moment: living in this fair golden city, he had by his wife Kamalai a steadfast daughter named Vimalai, whose colour outshines red gold and whose nature is like Fortune's.
1975.nuance: கம்பம் இலாதாள் (line 3), 'one without trembling', praises her steadiness before her beauty; the name விமலை, 'the stainless', is set beside her mother's name கமலை.
1975.event: Sagaradattan tells Civakan of his daughter Vimalai, born to his wife Kamalai.

1976.reading: He goes on: when this flower-doll was born, those who know what is to come wrote her fortune that very day, and he bids his hearer listen to what they said of the house and its goods.
1976.nuance: Line 3 (தும்பியாதும் இல்லாக் குளம் போன்றது என்று ஓம் இல் பண்டம்) seems to compare the house's stock to a pond, but the construction is obscure as divided; the vocative கூம்பாத செல்வக் கொடியே in line 4 is odd addressed to Civakan and may belong to the quoted prophecy.
1976.event: Sagaradattan recalls that at Vimalai's birth the astrologers wrote down her fortune.

1977.reading: The prophecy, as he reports it: the man fit for the girl will come up onto the shop, and when he does the ship-borne goods and stored wealth will all be taken at once; and the chest of that peerless man will be the maiden's fragrant flower-bed.
1977.nuance: The sign of the destined husband is a commercial one, fitted to a merchant's house: not a feat of arms or a contest, but goods that would not sell selling the moment he climbs onto the shop.
1977.event: Sagaradattan repeats the astrologers' sign: the destined husband will sit at the shop and its unsold cargo will sell at once.

1978.reading: Vimalai is now past seven years and two and two more; the wealth that would not sell has sold all at once for the master of the bow; it has come about as fated, so let him take the beauty of the girl with the slender waist and garlanded breasts, the merchant says.
1978.nuance: ஊழாயிற்று (line 3) makes the offer of the daughter an act of compliance with destiny rather than the father's choice. The age in line 1 (ஏழாண்டின் மேலும் இரண்டாண்டு இரண்டு) can be summed more than one way.
1978.event: Sagaradattan declares the prophecy fulfilled and offers Vimalai to Civakan.

claims.claim: what was foretold at birth has come to pass as destiny, so the marriage must follow

1979.reading: As if a bangle had dropped into an outstretched hand, the merchant duly assured the prince of the girl's great beauty, and the lady, seeing the prince, eased her pain and held on to her life.
1979.nuance: The simile in line 1 (ஏற்ற கைத்தொடி வீழ்ந்தென) and the subject of தேற்றினான் are unclear; the reading takes the merchant as the one who reassures.
1979.event: Civakan accepts the match, and Vimalai, seeing him, recovers from her lovesickness.

1980.reading: For the woman like a golden branch and the man like a red-gold hill with warrior anklets, the many instruments of the golden city sounded and the people made a joy unmatched on earth.
1980.event: Civakan and Vimalai are married amid the music of the whole city.

1981.reading: The handsome youth who mounted the bed and the lady of the honey-dripping garland never left each other, and so, joined, they became one life in two bodies.
1981.nuance: The oneness is given a cause, விட்டு நீங்குதல் இன்மையின், 'because they never parted': the formula holds only while they stay together, which the chapter's end tests.
1981.event: Civakan and Vimalai live together as one.

1982.reading: The fine cloth like white moonlight and the jewels did not hide her eyes for the burning, and they say the pleasure of the breasts of the woman with spear-like eyes is worth the three worlds.
1982.nuance: The valuation is hedged as hearsay (என்பவே, line 3). Line 2 (கலவங் கண்புதையாது கனற்றலின்) is compressed and the sense of the burning is uncertain.

1983.reading: The lady with the honey-scented garland and the youth with the spear that pierces enemies' flesh stayed on the soft bed fragrant as a forest, in the manner of the gods.
1983.event: Civakan and Vimalai spend their days in pleasure on the bridal bed.

1984.reading: In the long fine mansion whose walls bear the scars of rubbing against the white moon, mounting the couch in agil smoke, the doll-like girl tuned the strings of the makara vina and sang, and the man with drum-like shoulders was lost in delight.
1984.nuance: Civakan won Gandharvadattai by the vina; here the bride plays and he only listens.
1984.event: Vimalai plays the vina and sings for Civakan.

1985.reading: With her anklets and girdle-bells crying out against each other, her gold garland hanging, her flowered tresses loosened, her jewelled belt swelling and her eyes melting, he tasted the rich ripe fruit of desire and would not let go.

1986.reading: Her garland crushed against his breast and her silk disordered, the man of the honey-dripping garland held up wine in a jewelled cup to the lovely lady, who drank it sweetly and, plunged in the sea of desire, fell asleep.
1986.nuance: The epic, Jain by tradition, narrates the drinking of தேறல் in the bridal chamber without comment; no claim about drink is made here.
1986.event: Civakan offers Vimalai wine from a jewelled cup; she drinks and falls asleep.

1987.reading: When the youth, rolling betel leaves for her, touched the silk at her waist, the sleepy eyes of the girl with faultless breasts opened slowly, like a fragrant blue lily opening its mouth.
1987.event: Civakan wakes Vimalai with betel and a touch.

1988.reading: Calling him a thief who has crept in by night, she binds his forearm with the garland hanging from her hair and asks why he has come; he says he came hungry, and when she asks what he craves, he answers: the nectar of your beauty.
1988.nuance: The arrest is play: the garland is the rope, and the 'thief' confesses a hunger that is a compliment.
1988.event: Vimalai playfully binds Civakan as a night thief and questions him, and he answers that he hungers for her.

1989.reading: Feigning anger, she reddens and stares; he sets her small feet on his head and asks why she doubts and what grace she grants her servant; she tells the broad-chested one to hold his breath, say nothing, and stay on the flower-bed.
1989.nuance: Line 2 (அயிர்ப்பதென் பணிசெய்வேனுக்கு அருளிற்றுப் பொருளது) is divided obscurely; the reading takes it as Civakan's plea.
1989.event: Vimalai feigns anger, Civakan bows to her feet, and she bids him be silent and stay.

1990.reading: As the ghee within burned down and the light of the lovely lotus-shaped silver lamp grew faint, she became like a figure painted on the bed by a master's brush.
1990.nuance: The lamp running dry marks the end of the night that the next verse confirms.
1990.event: As the lamp burns low, Vimalai lies still as a painted picture.

1991.reading: The marutham-mode lute and flute the women played seemed to grieve that this prince would leave the lady today, so that all were troubled; the night went by and the morning's duties were done.
1991.nuance: The music knows what neither lover has said: the parting is announced first by the dawn melody (மருதம்), before Civakan speaks in 1993.
1991.event: At dawn the women's music sounds, as if lamenting that Civakan will leave Vimalai.

1992.reading: The man of the garlanded spear arranged her raised flower garlands, painted her young breasts with sandal so they shone, took her kanthal-bud fingers in his hand, and spoke to her.
1992.event: Civakan adorns Vimalai and takes her hand to speak to her.

1993.reading: He tells the woman of flower-hung tresses and body like mango shoots that he will go to the grove to see his friends and come back quicker than an arrow loosed from the bow.
1993.nuance: The promise of a return quicker than an arrow is made, but this chapter, the last of the ilampakam, does not show it kept.
1993.event: Civakan tells Vimalai he will go to see his companions in the grove and return at once.

1994.reading: When he said this, the pupils of her painted eyes swam in standing tears; he comforted the fragrant woman, and the man like a great jewel-hill went, while she, a creeper, drooped.
1994.event: Vimalai weeps; Civakan consoles her and leaves.

links.note: The sign written at Vimalai's birth, that the unsold cargo will sell when her husband climbs onto the shop, is the sale of 1973, made while Civakan sat lovesick at the shop front (1966).
links.teaches: The sale the merchant boasted of turns out to be a sign he had waited for since his daughter's birth, so Civakan's idle lovesick sitting is retold as the fulfilment of a prophecy he did not know.

links.note: Both brides have their husbands fixed by astrologers: Gandharvadattai's horoscope names the city where her destined groom lives (வந்தடை பான்மை), Vimalai's names the sign he will give.
links.teaches: Read together, the two horoscopes show the epic making each of Civakan's marriages a destiny read in advance, and fitting the sign to the father's world: a king's question about a place, a merchant's about goods that sell.

links.note: Here the narrator makes the couple one life in two bodies; in 1510 Kemasari, deserted, throws back at Civakan his own saying that love makes two lives one.
links.teaches: The oneness the narrator grants Vimalai is the formula Kemasari already turned against Civakan after he left her, so the reader knows before the dawn music that this union too ends in his going.

links.note: With Kemasari he rose while she slept and slipped out through the door unseen (1504-1505); with Vimalai he tells her he is going and promises a quick return.
links.teaches: Against the silent night escape from Kemasari, the open farewell to Vimalai looks kinder, yet it ends the same way in a departure, so the change lies in how he leaves, not in whether he stays.

links.note: The Kural's woman (or her friend) refuses a promise of speedy return: tell it to those who will still be alive. Civakan makes exactly that promise, quicker than an arrow, and Vimalai answers only with tears.
links.teaches: The epic stages the very speech the couplet refuses to accept, and the bride's silent tears in 1994 are the wordless form of the couplet's retort.

gains.a: Civakan's light promise is shown to be the stock comfort the Kural's speaker has already judged worthless.
gains.b: The couplet's retort gains a concrete farewell scene with the promise spelled out and a listener who cannot answer it.

links.note: The Kural's lover says his bond with the girl is that of body and life; the narrator says Civakan and Vimalai became one life in two bodies because they never parted.
links.teaches: The epic makes the couplet's body-and-life bond conditional on never parting, and then has the husband part at the next dawn, which tests the image the couplet offers as a pledge.

gains.a: The narrator's formula gains the force of a pledge, so his departure in 1994 reads as a breach of it.
gains.b: The couplet, a lover's pledge with no sequel, is given a sequel that shows what such a pledge is worth when the lover is a wanderer.

links.note: The narrator reports that the pleasure of Vimalai's breasts is worth the three worlds; the Naladiyar, a Jain didactic work, lists entrails, blood and bone and asks where among them the garlanded woman is.
links.teaches: The epic gives full voice to the valuation that the Jain didactic tradition exists to unmask, and hedges it as hearsay, so the praise stands as the worldly view that Civakan's later renunciation will have to undo.

gains.a: The hyperbole is placed as the very error a Jain reader is taught to dissolve, which gives it weight in the epic's arc toward renunciation.
gains.b: The quatrain's dissection gains a live instance of the praise it attacks, made within a work of the same religion.

source_issues: 1976 line 3 (தும்பியாது மில்லாக் குளம்போன்றதென் றோமில் பண்டங்) is obscure as divided, and the vocative in line 4 (கூம்பாத செல்வக் கொடியே) fits Civakan badly.
1978 line 1 (ஏழாண்டின் மேலு மிரண்டாண்டிரண் டெய்தி) gives Vimalai's age in a form that can be summed more than one way.
1979 line 1 (ஏற்ற கைத்தொடி வீழ்ந்தென) and the subject of தேற்றினான் in line 2 are unclear.
1982 line 2 (கலவங் கண்புதை யாது கனற்றலி) is compressed; the sense of the burning is uncertain.
1989 line 2 (அயிர்ப்பதென் பணிசெய் வேனுக் கருளிற்றுப் பொருள தென்ன) is divided obscurely.
1974 line 4 runs இல் and மாமனொடு together (நிலமாமனொ); read as இல் மாமனொடு.
